blocks.p: Now about this time their month was up, so they let the household know that it was time for them to be up and going. Then Joseph said to his mother, “Don’t forget to send to the house of Mr. Interpreter and ask him to let Mr. Great-heart be sent to us, to be our guide for the rest of the way.”

“Good boy,” she said. “I had almost forgotten.” So she wrote out a petition and asked Mr. Watchful, the porter, to send it by some suitable man to her good friend the Interpreter; and when it arrived and he had read its contents, he said to the messenger, “Go and tell them that I will send him.”

When the family Christiana was staying with saw that they meant to go forward, they called the whole house together to give thanks to their King for sending them such profitable guests. When this was done, they said to Christiana, “And shall we not show you something, as our custom is with pilgrims, that you may think over when you are on the road?” So they took Christiana, her children, and Mercy into a private room and showed them one of the apples that Eve ate, and gave to her husband, for the eating of which they were both turned out of Paradise; and they asked her what she thought it was.
“It is food or poison,” said Christiana, “I don’t know which.” So they explained the matter to her, and she lifted up her hands and wondered. [Gen. 3:6; Rom. 7:24]

Then they took her to a place and showed her Jacob’s ladder. At that moment there were angels going up it. So Christiana looked and looked, watching the angels climb, and so did the rest of the company. They were about to go to another place to show them something else, when James said to his mother, “Please ask them to stay here a little longer, for this is a wonderful sight.” So they turned back and stood feasting their eyes on that most pleasant prospect. [Gen. 28:12; John 1:51]

After this they took them to a place where a golden anchor hung, and they told Christiana to take it down. “For you shall have it with you,” they said; “it is absolutely necessary that you should, so that you may take hold of what is within the veil and stand steadfast if you meet with stormy weather.” And they were glad of it. [Heb. 6:19] Then they took them to the mount where Abraham our father offered up his son Isaac, and showed them the altar, the wood, the fire, and the knife, for they remain to be seen to this very day. [Gen. 22:9] When they had seen it, they lifted up their hands and blessed themselves, and said, “Oh, what a man Abraham was, for love to his Master and denial of himself!”

When they had shown them all these things, Prudence took them into the dining room, where there stood a fine pair of virginals; and she played on them, and turned what she had shown them into this excellent song:

v: Eve’s apple we have shown to you;
of that, then, be aware.
And Jacob’s ladder you’ve seen too,
with angels on the stair.
An anchor you have now received;
but let not these suffice
till you, like Abraham, have believed
and brought your best for sacrifice.

blocks.p: About this time someone knocked at the door; the porter opened it, and there stood Mr. Great-heart. And when he came in, what joy there was! For it came freshly to their minds how, only a little while ago, he had slain old Grim Bloody-man the giant, and delivered them from the lions.

Then Mr. Great-heart said to Christiana and Mercy, “My Lord has sent each of you a bottle of wine, and some roasted grain, and a couple of pomegranates. He has also sent the boys some figs and raisins, to refresh you on your way.”
Then they set out on their journey, and Prudence and Piety went along with them. When they came to the gate, Christiana asked the porter whether anyone had passed by lately.

“No,” he said, “only one, some time ago, who told me that a great robbery had recently been committed on the King’s highway, up ahead of you; but, he said, the thieves have been caught and will shortly be tried for their lives.”
Then Christiana and Mercy were afraid; but Matthew said, “Mother, fear nothing, as long as Mr. Great-heart is going with us to be our guide.”

Then Christiana said to the porter, “Sir, I am much obliged to you for all the kindness you have shown me since I came here, and for being so loving and kind to my children. I don’t know how to repay your kindness. So please accept this small gift as a token of my respect.” And she put a gold angel in his hand. He bowed low to her and said, “Let your garments be always white, and let your head never lack oil. Let Mercy live and not die, and let her works not be few.” And to the boys he said, “Flee youthful lusts, and follow godliness along with those who are serious and wise; so you will put gladness into your mother’s heart, and win the praise of all who are sober-minded.” So they thanked the porter and departed.

Now I saw in my dream that they went forward until they came to the brow of the hill, where Piety, remembering something, cried out, “Alas! I have forgotten what I meant to give Christiana and her companions. I will go back and fetch it.” So she ran and fetched it. While she was gone, Christiana thought she heard, in a grove a little way off to the right, a most wonderfully melodious song, with words much like these:

v: Through all my life your favor is
so freely shown to me,
that in your house forevermore
my dwelling place shall be.

blocks.p: And still listening, she thought she heard another answer it:

v: And why? The Lord our God is good;
his mercy is forever sure;
his truth at all times firmly stood,
and shall from age to age endure.

blocks.p: So Christiana asked Prudence what it was that made those lovely notes. “They are our country birds,” she said. “They sing these notes only rarely, except in the spring, when the flowers appear and the sun shines warm, and then you may hear them all day long. [Song 2:11-12] I often go out to hear them. We often keep them tame in our house too. They are very fine company for us when we are melancholy; and they make the woods and groves and lonely places into places one longs to be in.”

By this time Piety had come back. “Look,” she said to Christiana, “I have brought you a summary of all the things you have seen at our house, which you may look at when you find yourself forgetful, and so call those things back to mind for your instruction and comfort.”

Now they began to go down the hill into the Valley of Humiliation. It was a steep hill and the way was slippery; but they were very careful, and so they got down fairly well. When they were down in the valley, Piety said to Christiana, “This is the place where your husband Christian met the foul fiend Apollyon, and where they had that dreadful fight of theirs; I know you must have heard of it. But be of good courage: as long as you have Mr. Great-heart here to be your guide, we hope you will fare better.” So when these two had committed the pilgrims to the care of their guide, he went forward, and they went after him.

“We needn’t be so afraid of this valley,” said Mr. Great-heart, “for there is nothing here to hurt us unless we bring it on ourselves. It is true that Christian met Apollyon here, and had a hard fight with him; but that fight was the fruit of the slips he had coming down the hill, for those who slip there must expect fights here. That is how this valley has got such a bad name. The common people, when they hear that something frightful has happened to someone in some place, decide that the place is haunted by some foul fiend or evil spirit; when, alas, it is the fruit of their own doing that such things happen to them there.

“This Valley of Humiliation is in itself as fruitful a place as any the crow flies over; and I am persuaded that, if we look for it, we might find somewhere around here something that would tell us why Christian was so hard pressed in this place.”

Then James said to his mother, “Look, there stands a pillar over there, and it looks as if something is written on it. Let’s go and see what it says.” So they went, and found written there: Let Christian’s slips before he came here, and the battles he met with in this place, be a warning to those who come after.

“There,” said their guide, “didn’t I tell you there was something hereabouts that would hint at the reason Christian was so hard pressed in this place?” Then, turning to Christiana, he said, “This is no slur on Christian, any more than on many others whose lot has been the same; for it is easier going up this hill than down, and that can be said of few hills in all these parts of the world. But we will leave the good man; he is at rest, and he had a brave victory over his enemy. May he who dwells above grant that we fare no worse, when we come to be tried, than he did.

“But to come back to this Valley of Humiliation. It is the best and most useful piece of ground in all these parts. It is rich ground, and, as you see, mostly meadow; and if a man came here in summertime, as we do now, knowing nothing of it beforehand, and if he took delight in what his eyes could see, he would find things here to delight him. Look how green this valley is, and how beautiful with lilies. [Song 2:1] I have known many working men who have gained good estates in this Valley of Humiliation, ‘for God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble’ [James 4:6; 1 Pet. 5:5]; it is very fruitful soil indeed, and yields by the handful. Some have wished that the shortest way to their Father’s house ran through here, so that they might be troubled no more with hills and mountains to cross; but the way is the way, and there’s an end of it.”

Now, as they went along talking, they spotted a boy minding his father’s sheep. The boy was in very poor clothes, but had a fresh and good-looking face; and as he sat there by himself, he sang. “Listen,” said Mr. Great-heart, “to what the shepherd’s boy is saying.” So they listened, and he sang:

v: He that is down need fear no fall;
he that is low, no pride;
he that is humble ever shall
have God to be his guide. [Phil. 4:12-13]
I am content with what I have,
little be it, or much;
and, Lord, contentment still I crave,
because you save all such.
For pilgrims, all abundance is
a weight on pilgrimage;
here little, and hereafter bliss,
is best from age to age. [Heb. 13:5]

blocks.p: “Do you hear him?” said the guide. “I dare say that boy lives a merrier life, and wears more of that herb called heart’s-ease in his bosom, than the man who is dressed in silk and velvet. But let us go on with our talk.

“In this valley our Lord once had his country house. He loved to be here; he loved to walk these meadows too, for he found the air pleasant. Besides, here a man is free from the noise and the hurry of this life. Every other condition is full of noise and confusion; only the Valley of Humiliation is this empty, solitary place. Here a man is not so hindered in his contemplation as he tends to be elsewhere. This is a valley that nobody walks in except those who love a pilgrim’s life. And though Christian had the bad luck to meet Apollyon here and to enter into a sharp encounter with him, yet I must tell you that in former times men have met angels here, have found pearls here, and have found in this place the words of life. [Hos. 12:4-5]

“Did I say our Lord once had his country house here, and loved to walk here? I will add that to this place, and to the people who live here and walk these grounds, he has left a yearly revenue, to be faithfully paid them at certain seasons, for their support along the way and their further encouragement to go on with their pilgrimage.” [Matt. 11:29]
Now as they went on, Samuel said to Mr. Great-heart, “Sir, I understand that my father and Apollyon had their battle in this valley; but where exactly was the fight? For I see this valley is large.”

“Your father had that battle with Apollyon at a place ahead of us, in a narrow passage just beyond Forgetful Green. And indeed that place is the most dangerous in all these parts. For if pilgrims ever meet with a hard blow, it is when they forget what favors they have received and how unworthy they are of them. That is the place where others have been hard put to it too; but more about the place when we come to it, for I am convinced that to this day there remains some sign of the battle, or some monument to testify that such a battle was fought there.”

Then Mercy said, “I think I am as well off in this valley as I have been anywhere else on our whole journey. The place suits my spirit. I love to be in places where there is no rattling of coaches or rumbling of wheels. Here, it seems to me, one may think, without much disturbance, about what one is, where one came from, what one has done, and what the King has called one to; here one may think, and break at heart, and melt in spirit, until one’s eyes become like ‘the fishpools of Heshbon.’ [Song 7:4] Those who go rightly through this Valley of Baca make it a well; the rain that God sends down from heaven on those who are here also fills the pools. [Ps. 84:6-7] This is the valley from which the King will give his people their vineyards [Hos. 2:15]; and those who go through it will sing, as Christian did, for all that he met with Apollyon.”

“It is true,” said their guide. “I have gone through this valley many a time, and never was better than when I was here. I have also guided several pilgrims, and they have confessed the same. ‘To this man will I look,’ says the King, ‘to him who is poor and of a contrite spirit, and who trembles at my Word.’” [Isa. 66:2]

Now they had come to the place where the battle was fought. Then the guide said to Christiana, her children, and Mercy, “This is the place. On this ground Christian stood, and up there came Apollyon against him. And look, didn’t I tell you? Here is some of your husband’s blood on these stones to this day; see too, how here and there you can still find some of the splinters of Apollyon’s broken darts; see how they beat the ground with their feet as they fought, each to hold his position against the other; how, with their side blows, they split the very stones in pieces. Truly Christian played the man here, and showed himself as stout as Hercules himself would have been, had he been there. When Apollyon was beaten, he retreated to the next valley, called the Valley of the Shadow of Death, which we will come to soon.

“Look, there also stands a monument, on which this battle and Christian’s victory are engraved, to his fame through all ages.” Because it stood right by the wayside in front of them, they stepped up to it and read the writing, which word for word was this:

v: Hard by, here was a battle fought,
most strange, and yet most true:
Christian and Apollyon sought
each other to subdue.
The man so bravely played the man,
he made the fiend to fly;
of which a monument I stand,
the same to testify.
